Fur is natural, but think about where it comes from: almost all the fur sold today comes from farms where mink and foxes live in wire cages until they're killed. And being natural doesn't lower the impact: a 2011 CE Delft study found a higher environmental impact than textiles in 17 of 18 categories, because of feed and manure. The United Kingdom banned fur farms in 2000, and in 2020 Denmark culled about 15 million mink because of a coronavirus mutation. But the question remains: is a coat worth a whole life in a cage?

text.bold: 1. Life on the farms isn't natural.

paragraph.text: Mink, foxes and chinchillas are wild animals, with behaviors such as swimming, digging and roaming large areas, raised in wire cages.

CE Delft calculated that a mink eats almost 50 kg of feed over its life and that 1 kg of fur has a higher impact than cotton, acrylic, polyester and wool in 17 of 18 environmental categories, including climate change.

The United Kingdom banned fur farms in 2000, and several European countries followed. The farms have also become a health risk: in 2020, Denmark ordered the culling of all its farmed mink, about 15 million, after finding a coronavirus variant circulating among them.
Recycled, plant-based and second-hand fabrics provide warmth and durability without raising animals (H16).

text.bold: 5. Whoever condemns fur needs to explain food.

paragraph.text: Many people who don't consider themselves animal advocates oppose fur. Asked why, they tend to say it's wrong to make animals suffer and kill them for something we don't need. The philosopher Nathan Nobis notes that these reasons seem to apply to meat, milk and eggs as well, and that whoever uses them has three consistent ways out: revise their view on fur, revise their view on food, or point to a relevant difference between the two cases (

, 2016, p. 51). One difference often pointed out is that fur is a luxury and food a necessity. But for those with access to alternatives, animal-based food is also dispensable (G1), and the coat and the steak come from animals who spent their lives confined and were killed young. The same challenge applies to leather (I8).

In November 2020, after coronavirus variants were found in mink farmed for fur, Denmark announced the culling of every mink in the country, more than 17 million, in a decision that later faced legal challenges. Jeff Sebo (2022) notes that the debate dealt almost only with human costs, and that, when the animals were discussed, the only question was whether they should be killed: in an epidemic among humans, no one would think only of that. The case shows the risks these farms create and how little those who live in them are considered.
